A total charge \({Q}\) is divided into two parts, \({q}\) and \(({Q}-{q}),\) which are placed at a fixed distance apart. What value should \({q}\) have (in terms of \({Q}\)) so that the electrostatic repulsive force between the two charges is maximum?

Hint:\(F=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}\) Step 1: Find the electrostatic force between new charges. \(F=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}\) \(\Rightarrow F=\dfrac{kq(Q-q)}{r^2}\) \(\Rightarrow F=\dfrac{k}{r^2}(qQ-q^2)\) Step 2: Find the relation between charges\(q\text{ and }Q.\) For maximum or minimum values of electrostatic force: \(\dfrac{dF}{dq}=0\) \(\Rightarrow \dfrac{k}{r^2}(Q-2q)=0\) \(\Rightarrow (Q-2q)=0\) \(\Rightarrow Q=2q\) Hence, option (3) is the correct answer.

Two identical charged particles are suspended from a common point by light, inextensible threads, as shown in the figure. Due to electrostatic repulsion, the threads make equal angles \(\theta\) with the vertical. When the entire arrangement is immersed in a liquid, the angular separation between the two particles remains unchanged. The relative density of the particles is \(1.4,\) and the relative density of the liquid is \(0.7\cdot\) The dielectric constant of the liquid is:

1.\(5\)2.\(2\)
3.\(3\)4.\(1\)
questions.explanation:
Hint:The gravitational force is reduced due to buoyancy. Step:Find the dielectric constant of liquid. In air: \(T\sin\theta=F_e\) \(T\cos\theta=mg\) \(\Rightarrow \tan\theta=\dfrac{F_e}{mg}\) In liquid: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{F_e}{mg}=\dfrac{F_e/K}{mg-F_B}\) \(\Rightarrow \dfrac{F_e}{mg}=\dfrac{F_e/K}{mg-F_B}\) \(\Rightarrow \dfrac{K}{mg}=\dfrac{1}{mg-\rho_LVg}\) \(\Rightarrow \dfrac{K}{mg}=\dfrac{1}{mg-\rho_L\dfrac{m}{\rho_{\text{particles}}}g}\) \(\Rightarrow K=\dfrac{1}{1-\rho_L/\rho_{\text{particles}}}\) \(\Rightarrow K=\dfrac{1}{1-0.7/1.4}\) \(\Rightarrow K=2\) Hence, option (2) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Two electrons are fixed at a distance of \(2d\) apart. A proton is placed at the midpoint between them and is displaced slightly by a distance \(x\) \((x\ll d)\) perpendicular to the line joining the two fixed electrons. The proton will undergo simple harmonic motion with an angular frequency given by:
(here, \(m\) is the mass of the proton, \(q\) is the magnitude of the charge, and \(\varepsilon_0\)​ is the permittivity of free space)

1. \(\sqrt{\left( {\dfrac{2 q^2}{\pi \varepsilon_0 m d^3}}\right)}~\)

2. \(\sqrt{\left (\dfrac{\pi \varepsilon_0 {md}^3}{2 {q}^2} \right )}~\)

3. \(\sqrt{\left ({\dfrac{ q^2}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 m d^3}}\right)}~\)

4. \(\sqrt{\left( \dfrac{2\pi \varepsilon_0 {md}^3}{m{q}^2}\right)}~\)
questions.explanation:
Hint:\(a=\omega^2x\) Step: Find the angular frequency by which the proton will undergo simple harmonic motion. From the given condition, we have; The forces on the proton due to the two electrons are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction along the line joining the electrons. Only the perpendicular components of these forces contribute to the net restoring force. The force due to a single electron at a distance \(r\) from the proton is given by; \(\Rightarrow F = \frac{q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}\) If the proton is displaced perpendicular to the line joining the electrons by a distance \(x,\) the distance from the proton to each electron, it becomes: \(\Rightarrow r = \sqrt{d^2 + x^2} \approx d \quad (\text{since } x \ll d)\) The perpendicular component of the force due to one electron is given by; \(\Rightarrow F_{⊥} = F \times \frac{x}{r} = \frac{q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} \times \frac{x}{r}\) Substituting \(r \approx d\)we get; \(\Rightarrow F_{\perp} = \frac{q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 d^2} \times \frac{x}{d} = \frac{q^2 x}{4\pi\epsilon_0 d^3}\) The net restoring force is doubled because both electrons contribute that is defined by; \(\Rightarrow F_{\text{net}} = 2F_{\perp} = \frac{2q^2 x}{4\pi\epsilon_0 d^3}\) The equation of motion for the proton is given by; \(\Rightarrow F_{\text{net}} = -kx\) \(\Rightarrow k = \frac{2q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 d^3}\) The angular frequency \(\omega\) of simple harmonic motion is given by; \(\Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\) \(\Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{2q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 d^3}}{m}}= \sqrt{\frac{q^2}{2\pi\epsilon_0 m d^3}}\) Hence, option (3) is the correct answer.​​​

Two identical conducting spheres, each with negligible volume, carry initial charges of \(2.1~\text{nC}\) and \(-0.1~\text{nC},\) respectively. The spheres are brought into contact, allowing charge to redistribute, and are then separated by a distance of \(0.5~\text m.\) The electrostatic force acting between the spheres is:
\(\left ( 4 \pi \varepsilon_0=\frac{1}{9 \times 10^9}~\text{in SI units} \right )\)
1. \(36 \times 10^{-7}~\mathrm{N}\)
2. \(36 \times 10^{-9}~\mathrm{N}\)
3. \(18 \times 10^{-7}~\mathrm{N}\)
4. \(18 \times 10^{-9}~\mathrm{N}\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: The charge gets equally distributed when both of them are in contact. Step: Find the electrostatic force acting between the spheres​​​​​.When the spheres are brought into contact, the charges redistribute equally because the spheres are identical. The total charge is given by; \(\Rightarrow q_{\text{total}} = q_1 + q_2 = (2.1 - 0.1) \, \text{nC} = 2.0 \, \text{nC}\) After contact, the charge on each sphere is given by; \(\Rightarrow q_{\text{final}} = \frac{q_{\text{total}}}{2} = \frac{2.0}{2} \, \text{nC} = 1.0 \, \text{nC} = 1.0 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C}\) The spheres are separated by a distance \(r=0.5~\text m\). The electrostatic force between the spheres is given by Coulomb's law; \(\Rightarrow F = \frac{k q_1 q_2}{r^2}\) \(\Rightarrow F = \frac{9 \times 10^9 (1.0 \times 10^{-9})(1.0 \times 10^{-9})}{(0.5)^2}\) \(\Rightarrow F = \frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-18}}{0.25}\) \(\Rightarrow F= \frac{9 \times 10^{-9}}{0.25} = 36 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{N}\) Hence, option (2) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
In finding the electric field using Gauss law the formula \(|\vec{E}|=\dfrac{q_{\text {enc }}}{\varepsilon_0|A|}\) is applicable. In the formula \(\varepsilon_0\) is the permittivity of free space, \(A\) is the area of the Gaussian surface and \(q_{e n c}\) is the charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface. 2.for any choice of Gaussian surface.
3.only when \(|\vec{E}|\)= constant on the surface.
4.only when the Gaussian surface is an equipotential surface.
questions.explanation:
Hint: The electric field is always perpendicular to the equipotential surface. Explanation:The formula \(|\vec E| = \dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0 |A|}\) ​​ follows from Gauss’s law only when the chosen Gaussian surface is such that the electric field is everywhere perpendicular to the surface and has the same magnitude at all points on it. An equipotential surface satisfies the first requirement because electric field lines are always normal to equipotential surfaces, and in symmetric charge distributions the magnitude of the field also remains constant over that surface. Under these conditions, \(\vec E \cdot d\vec A = |\vec E|\, dA\)everywhere on the surface, allowing \(|\vec E|\)to be taken out of the integral and leading directly to the given formula. Hence, the equation is applicable when the Gaussian surface is an equipotential surface and \(|\vec E|\) is constant on it. Hence, option (1) is the correct answer.
